opus-5.5.text:
I think the principle has to be very simple: if your name is on it, you own it. It doesn't matter whether you wrote every line yourself, whether a student helped you, or whether an AI agent produced ninety percent of it. When you submit a proof to a journal or a pull request to a codebase, you are vouching for it. That's always been the social contract in mathematics and in engineering, and I don't think AI changes it. If anything, it makes it more important.

What AI does change is the economics. It's now incredibly cheap to generate something that *looks* like a proof or *looks* like working code. Producing a plausible twenty-page argument used to take weeks of effort, and that effort was itself a kind of filter. Now that filter is gone. So if people start submitting things they haven't checked, the burden shifts entirely onto reviewers, referees, and maintainers. Their time is the scarce resource, and it's not fair to flood them with unverified output.

So my view is: use the agents, absolutely. I use them every day, and they're becoming genuinely useful for research-level mathematics. But before you submit, you have to understand the work well enough to defend it. If a referee asks you about step seven, "the model did it" is not an answer. You should be able to explain why step seven is true.

I'd also strongly encourage transparency. Say how you used AI, not as a confession, but because it helps people calibrate. And where possible, lean on verification. In code that means tests and review. In math, formal proof assistants like Lean are becoming more practical, and I think the combination of AI generating proofs and machines checking them is going to be a very powerful way to keep trust intact as the volume goes up.

Ultimately, AI is a tool. An extraordinary one, but a tool. Responsibility stays with the human who decides to put the work out into the world.

r001.rationale: It says the person submitting the work owns and vouches for it, regardless of how much an AI agent produced.

r002.rationale: It places responsibility on submitters and discusses checking work, but does not advocate stronger reputational accountability for people who publish incorrect proofs.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the principle has to be very simple: if you put your name on it, you own it. The agent is a tool. A very powerful tool, maybe soon a tool that is smarter than you in some narrow sense, but it doesn't sign the paper, it doesn't get the credit, and so it also cannot take the blame.

What I've seen, in mathematics especially, is a temptation to say, "well, the model produced this proof, I checked it a little bit, and I'm submitting it." And then if there's a gap, the implicit excuse is, "the AI made a mistake." I think that's not acceptable. The whole point of the author being a human is that a human stands behind the claim. If you didn't understand the proof well enough to defend it, you shouldn't have submitted it. Or at the very least you should be transparent and say, "here is a proof that was generated, I have verified this part, this part I have not."

Now, the good news in math and in code is that we actually have mechanisms that make this tractable. For code, you have tests, you have review, you have the fact that the thing runs or doesn't run. For math, we have formal verification. If something is checked in Lean, then honestly I care much less who or what wrote it, because the responsibility question becomes almost trivial. The proof is correct, period. So part of my answer is that the responsibility of the human shifts. It becomes less about verifying every line by hand, and more about choosing the right verification process and being honest about what was and wasn't verified.

There is also a question of disclosure. I think we are in a transition period where it genuinely matters for the community to know how much of a result came from an AI system. Not because it diminishes the result, but because it tells referees and readers where to look, and because it helps us collectively learn what these systems are good and bad at. In a few years, this may feel as silly as disclosing that you used a calculator. But today, I would err on the side of saying what you did.

And finally, I'd say responsibility goes the other way too. If you use an agent and it finds something genuinely new, you should be generous in describing that. Pretending you did everything yourself is also a kind of dishonesty. So, the human owns the errors, the human is honest about the process, and the verification tools do the heavy lifting. That seems like the right equilibrium to me.

r001.rationale: It says the human who puts their name on the work owns it and cannot blame the agent for errors.

r002.rationale: It says authors should stand behind proofs and not submit work they cannot defend, but it does not advocate stronger reputational accountability for publishing incorrect proofs.

astra-6.text:
I think the person submitting the work has to take responsibility for it. If you submit a mathematical proof, you should understand the argument and be able to defend it. Saying, “Well, the AI told me this was true,” cannot be enough. The same applies to code: you need to have a basis for trusting that it does what you claim it does.

That doesn’t mean you have to reproduce every step the agent took. We already rely on tools and on other people’s work. But you need verification appropriate to the claim. Tests can give you evidence about code; for mathematics, you need a valid proof, perhaps one that can be checked formally. The agent can help you get there, but it doesn’t remove your responsibility when you put your name on the result.

r001.rationale: The response says the person submitting AI-assisted mathematics or code is responsible for it and must be able to justify or verify the result.

r002.rationale: It requires submitters to take responsibility, but does not advocate stronger reputational accountability for people who publish incorrect mathematical proofs.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the person submitting the work has to take responsibility for it. If you submit a mathematical proof, you’re saying, “I believe this proof is correct, and I can defend it.” The fact that an AI helped you find it doesn’t remove that obligation. You have to check the argument, understand where the assumptions enter, and be honest about anything you haven’t verified.

For code, it’s similar. Getting an agent to produce something that looks plausible is not the same as establishing that it works. You’re responsible for reviewing it and testing it appropriately for how it will be used.

That doesn’t mean you have to reproduce every step of the agent’s process. But you need a sound basis for trusting the result. “The AI told me so” is not enough.

r001.rationale: The response says the person submitting AI-assisted mathematics or code is responsible for it and must review, understand, or test the result.

r002.rationale: It calls for checking and defending proofs but does not advocate stronger reputational accountability for people who publish incorrect proofs.
